nodes.body: Wren Callahan can't sleep. She climbs the ladder to the attic, where her late grandfather's shortwave radio sits under a dust sheet like something waiting to be woken up. She switches it on anyway, the way she has every night for a week now. Out of the hiss comes the same loop she heard last night: a young woman's flat, careful voice reading a string of numbers, over and over, then a slow tone that counts downward and resets, starting the whole cycle again from the top. It should sound like nothing, an old machine talking to itself in an empty room. Instead it sounds like a door left open on purpose, waiting for someone to walk through it.

choices.label: Let the loop run once more.

nodes.body: While the numbers run, her eyes go where they always go, to the two things of his that she has never touched. On the shelf above the radio sits his spare battery, wrapped in a rag and labeled in his square capitals: JUST IN CASE. On a hook beside it hangs his operator's headset, the heavy one with the cracked leather pads and the name Callahan inked inside the band. He swore that it could let you hear the room behind a voice. Wren is the only one who still comes up here, and she has dusted around both of them for a year, because moving anything of his felt like agreeing that he was gone. Tonight the loop sounds too much like a question to sit still for. She makes herself a bargain: she is allowed to take down one thing of his, and only one.

choices.label: Take down the spare battery.
Lift his headset off its hook.

nodes.body: The battery is heavier than it looks, and colder. She unwraps it far enough to check the terminals, which are still bright under a year of dust. Then she wraps it again and lowers it into the bottom of her pack. The straps dig into her shoulders when she shrugs the pack on, and for no sensible reason the extra weight makes her feel a little less alone up here.

choices.label: Turn back to the radio.

nodes.body: She lifts the headset off its hook, and the old leather creaks as if it remembers being worn. It smells like him, like solder and peppermint, and for a second she only holds it. When she plugs it in and pulls it down over her ears, the attic drops away completely. The hiss grows deeper and wider, like the darkness inside a very big room, and the woman's voice steps out of it so close that Wren almost turns around.

choices.label: Turn back to the radio.

nodes.body: Three things pull at her at once, in three different directions. The numbers might be coordinates, if she copied them onto graph paper and treated them as a map, the way her grandfather taught her on wet weekends. The relay station out on the headland has stood dark for as long as she can remember, yet a signal this steady has to be coming from somewhere real. And he kept a logbook of everything he ever heard on this radio, every night for forty years. If this loop is in it, then he knew about it, and he never said. The voice starts again from the top, and Wren finds that she is already reaching for her shoes.

choices.label: Plot the numbers as coordinates.
Bike out to the relay station.
Hunt for Grandpa's logbook.

nodes.body: She plots the numbers as coordinates at the kitchen table, in pairs, latitude and then longitude, the way he showed her. Most of the string makes no sense as a place, but two of the pairs do. One falls on the working harbor at the bottom of the hill, where the lights stay on all night for the boats. The other falls on the old water tower up on the headland ridge, which she has ridden past since she was small enough for training wheels. They lie in opposite directions, a mile and a half apart. Wren clips her handheld radio to her belt and sees that its battery light has already turned amber. "One of you, then," she tells the two pencil crosses, "and no changing my mind halfway."

choices.label: Head down to the harbor.
Climb to the ridge water tower.

nodes.body: The harbor is asleep, with nothing moving but the ropes ticking against the masts and one gull complaining out on the breakwater. Wren holds her graph paper up to the sodium lights. The pencil cross sits between two buildings. One is the harbormaster's hut, where a single window still burns yellow. The other is the tide-gauge shed at the root of the breakwater, which everybody says was shut down before she was born. Halfway between them stands the pier notice-board, layered with flyers gone the color of driftwood. Her sneakers are already soaked through from the dew on the boards. The handheld crackles on her belt, and the voice begins the numbers again, a little louder than it was at the top of the hill.

choices.label: Knock at the harbormaster's hut.
Cross to the tide-gauge shed.
Check the pier notice-board.

nodes.body: The notice-board is a graveyard of old paper: a lost cat from three summers back, a bake sale nobody remembers, tide times bleached almost white. One index card does not belong. It is newer than everything round it, unfaded, and pinned dead in the center of the board instead of being buried under a decade of flyers. A single frequency is written across it in small careful handwriting, and beneath the numbers are eight words: if you hear the loop, it is real. Wren's pulse picks up as she reads it a second time. Somebody put this here on purpose, for a stranger, on the chance that a night like this one would come.

choices.label: Lean in close to the card.

nodes.body: Up close, the frequency on the card matches the loop, decimal for decimal, and the ink along one edge is still faintly damp. It has not been out here a day. Wren reads the eight words again: if you hear the loop, it is real. Whoever wrote that knew there would be someone, some night, who needed telling. But was it meant for her? She is only a girl who could not sleep, and this looks like a careful message to a person somebody was expecting. The wind is already working at one corner of the card, lifting it and letting it fall, and the pin that holds it is rusty enough to snap.

choices.label: Unpin the card and follow its frequency.
Leave the card for whoever it was meant for.

nodes.body: She unpins the card before the wind can have it, and tunes the handheld to the frequency written there, digit by digit. The loop leaps out of the little speaker twice as loud as it has ever been in the attic. Whoever wrote the card knew where on the dial to stand. When Wren turns in a slow circle on the wet boards, the signal swells in one direction only: north, along the shore, toward the headland. She slides the card into her back pocket, next to the graph paper.

choices.label: Follow the signal north along the shore.

nodes.body: She leaves the card for whoever it was meant for, since a message pinned up that carefully is not hers to take, and the wind has it off the board before she reaches the end of the pier. The next evening she goes back, feeling foolish. A new card is pinned in the same place, in the same small handwriting, and its ink is still wet. Somebody in this town replaces that card every time it blows away, and has been doing it since before the board was last painted. Wren waits by the railing until her feet go numb, and nobody comes. It is nearly midnight when she climbs to the attic, and there is only hiss where the numbers used to be. The loop was real, exactly as the card said, and it ended while she stood guard over a rusty pin.

She knocks at the harbormaster's hut, and Mr. Pell opens the door in a cable-knit sweater, more curious than cross at a caller this late, and listens to the handheld with his head on one side, the way people listen to a tune they half remember. "Well, I'll be salted," he says. "That used to come off the old relay out on the headland, back before the county pulled its money, and I thought it had stopped years ago." He rubs his jaw. "Whoever kept that going is as stubborn as barnacles, and I could put a name to him, but it is not my name to hand to a child at midnight, so you did not hear the headland from me." He has pointed straight at it all the same, and both of them know it.

choices.label: Thank him and take the headland road.

nodes.body: The tide-gauge shed sits at the root of the breakwater with a padlock rusted solid through its hasp, but one window is cracked open far enough to see through. On a shelf inside, among the cobwebs, a small receiver is switched on, and its green light is blinking in time with the loop. Wren presses closer to the glass. This shed is supposed to have been dead for years, yet somebody has left that thing listening, with its frequency written on a strip of tape along the top. The door beside her is so swollen with damp that it has sprung half out of its frame. One good shove would probably finish it, with a noise the whole harbor could hear.

choices.label: Shove the swollen door open.
Copy the frequency off the tape and go home.

nodes.body: She shoves the swollen door, and it opens with a groan that seems to go on for a week. Wren stands frozen in the doorway until she is sure that the light in the harbormaster's hut has not moved. Inside, the little receiver is wired to a solar panel on the roof and to a card taped on the wall beside it, hand-lettered in block capitals gone soft with damp: RELAY KX. So this shed is not the source of anything. It is an ear. Somebody rigged it up years ago to catch a signal that starts somewhere else, further out, where the land runs into the sea, and somebody has kept it working ever since. She pulls the door shut behind her as gently as she can, which is not very.

choices.label: Head along the shore toward the headland.

nodes.body: She copies the frequency off the tape into her notebook, under tonight's date, and walks home feeling sensible. Breaking into a shed at midnight is not a plan, and she means to come back with a better one. In the attic she turns the big dial to check the number against the loop, and her hand stops. There is a pencil tick on the glass on that spot, worn dark by years of thumbs. Her grandfather had marked it. He sat in this chair and listened to this same voice, and in all those years he never said one word about it to anyone. Wren writes WHY across the top of a clean page and leaves it for the weekend. By the weekend the tick is pointing at nothing but hiss, and the only person who could have told her is a year dead.

The water tower stands rust red against the stars, with a stub of broken antenna still bolted to its cap like a crooked crown. Up here the loop comes through the handheld stronger than it has all night, so sharp that Wren can follow the numbers without her notes. Something on this tower is catching the signal and throwing it on. A maintenance ladder runs straight up the side of the tank toward the antenna, its rungs flaking, with no cage round it and nothing underneath it but concrete. At the foot of the tower a steel service box is bolted to the pad, with a cable as thick as her wrist running out of it. The wind up here does not gust. It leans, all the time, like a hand in the middle of her back.

choices.label: Start up the ladder toward the antenna.
Look over the service box at the foot of the tower.

nodes.body: She starts up the ladder toward the antenna, and by the eighth rung she knows it was a mistake. The wind gets under her jacket and pulls, flakes of rust come away in her palms, and the rung under her left foot gives a small, sick click. Wren locks both arms round the rail and stays exactly where she is, cheek against the cold metal, with her heart banging in her throat. She does not go one rung higher. From here, though, she can see what she came for: a thin cable running off the antenna mount and away along the ridge, post after post, toward a black shape crouched on the point, which can only be the relay station. She climbs down a great deal more slowly than she went up, and sits on the concrete until her legs stop shaking.

choices.label: Follow the cable to the relay.

nodes.body: The service box at the foot of the tower is furred orange with rust, and its hinges have frozen solid. One panel has sprung at a corner, loose enough to pry at with the edge of her house key. Whatever is inside might tell her what this tower is doing with the signal, and it might also eat the rest of the night and a knuckle or two. Beside the box, on the concrete pad, somebody once stenciled an arrow in paint that has faded to the color of the rust. It points away along the ridge. A few yards further on there is another, and beyond that the pale line of a path, heading for the black bulk of the headland.

choices.label: Pry the rusted panel open.
Follow the stenciled arrows along the ridge.

nodes.body: She pries the rusted panel open with the edge of her house key, and it lets go with a shriek that seems far too loud for an empty ridge. Inside is a junction box in a nest of wiring. A laminated tag is zip-tied to the thickest cable, lettered in careful capitals: KX RELAY, HEADLAND, DO NOT DISCONNECT. Somebody cared enough about this connection to label it, and then to seal the label in plastic against years of salt. So the tower is only a repeater. It catches the signal and passes it along without adding a word of its own. The real transmitter is further out, where that cable goes, and Wren sucks her skinned knuckle and looks along the ridge after it.

choices.label: Head for the headland relay.

nodes.body: She follows the stenciled arrows along the ridge, counting them, and stops counting at nineteen. The path they mark is cracked asphalt, just wide enough for a service truck, and it hugs the high ground all the way out toward the headland. Whoever painted these wanted them followed in the dark by somebody in a hurry, because each arrow has a dab of reflective paint at its tip that catches her flashlight and winks. As she walks, the loop steadies in her earbuds. It no longer feels like something drifting about in the air. It feels like a road, laid down one arrow at a time for whoever was patient enough to walk it.

choices.label: Keep following the path.

nodes.body: The lights of the town fall behind her, and after that there is only the track along the headland, pale under the moon, and the sound of her own breathing. Wren keeps the handheld radio in her fist with the volume turned low. With every hundred yards the loop grows cleaner, the hiss thinning out from around the numbers until the woman's voice might be coming from the next room. Her graph paper is folded in her back pocket, and she no longer needs it. The numbers were never a map of the town. They were a hand pointing out past the edge of it, to where the land narrows and the old relay station stands on the point.

choices.label: Keep walking toward the point.

nodes.body: The track ends at a wind-scoured overlook, where the grass lies flat and the point is spread out below her. The relay station is not dark. A red lamp burns at the top of the mast, and in the long low building at its foot, one window is lit a warm yellow. Wren stands there until the wind has found its way inside her jacket. Then she goes down, because there is a footpath, and because the fence does not run along the cliff side, where nobody ever expected a visitor. She crosses the wet yard bent low, her heart going like a fist on a door, and stops beside the lit window with her back against the wall.

choices.label: Look through the lit window.

nodes.body: She bikes out to the relay station instead, because some mysteries have to be solved with legs. The headland road is empty this late, with only the thin cone of her headlamp and the wind coming steadily off the water. The station squats at the cliff edge with its mast like a black needle against the moon, as unwelcoming as every kid in town has always said. Wren stops where the road ends at a chained gate, and gets her breath back. To the right a footpath follows the fence along the cliff top, out in the open, with the surf a long way below it. To the left a service lane dips round behind the buildings, low and sheltered and shining with standing water. The loop in her earbuds is so loud that she turns it down.

choices.label: Take the coast path along the fence.
Take the service lane behind.

nodes.body: The coast path runs a hand's width from the chain-link fence, and on its other side the ground ends, in a long drop to the surf. The wind out here is vicious. It shoves at Wren sideways, hard enough that she has to plant her feet after every step, and twice it lifts the front wheel of the bicycle clean off the ground. Ahead of her the fence has peeled back from one of its posts, leaving a gap just wide enough for a determined body. The loop is louder here than it has been all night. Her phone is in her jacket pocket, and from this spot the mast stands clear against the moon, close enough to photograph.

choices.label: Slip through the peeled-back gap.
Photograph the mast and turn back.

nodes.body: She slips through the peeled-back gap in the chain-link, leaving a little skin from one elbow on the wire, and stands up inside the compound for the first time in her life. A weather-blistered sign leans against the fence, its paint gone the color of old rust: RELAY KX. Nothing in here looks abandoned. The weeds along the path have been cut, a coil of new cable sits under a tarpaulin by the wall, and somewhere a generator is ticking over as steadily as a clock. Wren presses her sleeve against her stinging elbow. Every kid in town knows this place is dead, and every kid in town is wrong.

choices.label: Go further into the compound.

nodes.body: She photographs the mast three times with shaking hands, while a gust does its best to lift her off the path, and then she turns the bicycle round. Nobody who had seen that drop would call it cowardly. At home, under the covers, she swipes through the pictures, and the first two show a black tower against a blacker sky. The third is blurred, but along its bottom edge there is a yellow window, and in the window the shape of a man holding a mug. So somebody lives out there. Wren decides to go back at the weekend, in daylight, by the sheltered lane behind the station. The loop does not wait for the weekend. It stops the very next night, in the middle of a number, and the man with the mug is the only answer she ever gets.

The service lane runs half under water, with the sea sheeting silver across the cracked asphalt, but the buildings keep the worst of the wind off her. Wren leaves the bicycle against a post and goes on by foot. Ahead on the left a gatehouse window glows with the light of a desk lamp, and through the glass she can make out a wall board covered from edge to edge in handwriting. Beyond it a squat transformer hut is humming, louder than the tide. Past the hut, a flight of stone steps goes down to a cellar doorway, and there is water moving at the bottom of them. Somewhere a gutter drips, one slow drop at a time, and nothing else in the place makes a sound.

choices.label: Try the gatehouse and its log board.
Wade to the humming transformer hut.
Go down the steps to the cellar doorway.

nodes.body: She goes down the steps to the cellar doorway, and at the bottom the sea is already over her ankles, cold enough to hurt. The air is thick with brine and rust and old engine oil. On the far wall, just above a dark tide line, somebody has taped a plastic sleeve with a single folded sheet of paper inside it, pale against the stone. Wren wades two steps closer. Every wave that booms against the sea wall outside sends a fresh pulse of water down the stairs behind her, and the level round her legs climbs a finger's width each time. This is a stupid place to be standing. She can read the first word through the plastic from here, and the first word is LOOP.

choices.label: Wade close enough to read it.

nodes.body: The note inside the sleeve is a single line, in block capitals that have run a little at the edges: LOOP STAYS UP WHILE I DRAW BREATH, signed with two letters, KX. Wren's hands are shaking, and not only from the cold. Somebody pinned a promise above the tide line, where he must have known the sea would come for it sooner or later, and the sea is coming now. The water has climbed from her ankles to her knees while she was reading. Another wave booms against the wall outside, and a fresh sheet of it runs down the steps behind her. The sleeve hangs an arm's length away, held to the stone by four strips of old tape.

choices.label: Wade in and peel the note off the wall.
Get back up the steps while she can.

nodes.body: She salvages the note, and it very nearly costs more than it is worth. The tape gives on the third pull and the sleeve comes away in her fist, and in the same second a wave slams the sea wall and the water in the cellar jumps from her knees to her waist. The cold knocks the breath out of her. She gets one hand on the rail and hauls herself up the steps with the surge dragging at her legs, and behind her the cellar fills to the place where the note was hanging. In the yard she stands shaking, soaked to the ribs. It is a full minute before her hands will work well enough to push the sleeve into her pocket.

choices.label: Get out of the wind.

nodes.body: She gets back up the steps two at a time, and she has barely reached the top when a wave booms against the sea wall and the cellar fills behind her like a bath. The plastic sleeve tears loose and goes under. Wren stands in the yard with her heart banging, looking down at black water where she was standing ten seconds ago, and she does not feel slow in the least. She has the words, in any case, because she read them: LOOP STAYS UP WHILE I DRAW BREATH. Somebody out here means to keep this signal alive until he dies. But her shoes are full of the sea and her teeth will not stop chattering, and by morning she is running a fever. She spends three days in bed, and when she can climb to the attic again, the loop is not there.

She tries the gatehouse door, and it opens on a room so warm that somebody must have stepped out a minute ago, meaning to come straight back. The log board fills one wall with line after line in the same careful hand, running back for years across the peeling paint, and the last entry looks only hours old. Wren leans in to read it, forgetting where she is. Then, somewhere out in the dark, a dog begins to bark. It is not close yet, but it is the bark of a dog that has heard something it does not like and is coming to see. The newest page of the log is held to the board by a single clip, level with her hand.

choices.label: Stay and read the log board.
Take the newest page and run.

nodes.body: She stays and reads the log board, with the barking drawing slowly nearer. The entries run decades deep, dates and frequencies and small notes in the margins that read almost like a diary. The last forty lines all say the same thing: LOOP HOLDING, STILL NO ANSWER. Wren reads that three times before it goes in. No machine writes LOOP HOLDING in tired handwriting, and no machine underlines STILL NO ANSWER as if the words had cost something. A person is tending this signal, night after night, and waiting to hear back from somebody who has never replied. The barking stops right outside the door. A lead rattles, a man's voice says, "Leave it, boy, there's nobody there," and the footsteps go away again.

choices.label: Slip back out into the yard.

nodes.body: She takes the newest page and runs, out of the door and along the lane, with the barking swinging round behind her. She does not stop until the gatehouse lamp is a yellow dot, and then she smooths the page out against her knee and reads the last line on it by the light of her phone: FOR M, STILL HOLDING. Four words, and the whole night rearranges itself round them. Nobody is looping numbers into the dark for no reason. It is a message with a name on it, or at least a letter, and whoever writes that log has been waiting a long time for an answer. Wren folds the page very small. She has stolen a piece of somebody's patience, and she is not at all sure that she had the right.

choices.label: Creep back toward the yard.

nodes.body: She wades to the humming transformer hut through water that comes over her ankles, and lays her palm flat against its door. The building is alive under her hand, feeding power to the mast overhead. A maintenance sticker is fixed beside the lock, curling at the edges, and her flashlight finds the last line on it: SERVICED BY K. ALDER. The date beside the name is last month's. Above that line are dozens more in the same careful hand, month after month and year after year, all the way to the top of the sticker. The technician Alder, whoever he is, did not walk away when the county did. He is still coming out here with his toolbox, and by the look of it he has never missed a month.

choices.label: Follow the power cable toward the mast.

nodes.body: Rain begins, thin and cold, needling the back of her neck. Across the yard, under the mast, stands a long low building with every window dark but one. That one glows a steady yellow, and each time the loop in her earbuds reaches the bottom of its count, a small red lamp beside it blinks, as if the building were breathing. Nobody leaves a lamp burning in a station the county shut down. Nobody sweeps a doorstep that nobody uses, and even from here she can see that the step under that window has been swept. Wren wipes the rain off her face with her sleeve. She has come all this way on a bicycle, in the dark, for a voice reading numbers, and the voice is coming from in there.

choices.label: Cross the yard toward the light.

nodes.body: She crosses the yard at a crouch, keeping to the puddled shadow along the fence, and nothing stops her. No dog comes, and no door opens. The mast hums overhead like a wire in the wind, and the red lamp on the wall keeps time with the loop, on at the top of the count and off at the bottom. Up close the building is smaller than it looked, more like a cabin than a station, with a rain barrel under the gutter and a pair of boots on the step. Wren stops beside the lit window with her back flat against the wall. She came out here to find a machine, and machines do not own boots.

choices.label: Look through the lit window.

nodes.body: She hunts for her grandfather's logbook instead of chasing the signal out into the dark. He listened to these airwaves for forty years, and he wrote down every contact and every odd frequency in his cramped square hand. If anybody heard this loop before she did, he heard it, and if he heard it, he logged it. He kept the things he valued in the cedar trunk at the far end of the attic, under the eaves. He kept the things he was still working on out in his radio shed, where a wall of pinned notes has hung untouched since the week he died. Wren stands at the top of the attic ladder with the flashlight in her teeth. She is looking for a dead man's handwriting to explain a signal that is very much alive.

choices.label: Open the cedar trunk in the attic.
Search the radio shed.

nodes.body: The cedar trunk breathes out the smell of old paper the moment she lifts its lid, and for a second he is standing right behind her. On top lies a logbook with a water-stained cover gone as soft as cloth. Beside it is a fat bundle of QSL cards in a rubber band, the postcards that radio operators send one another to prove a signal got through. Underneath both, almost hidden, is a stack of envelopes tied with a ribbon, addressed in his writing and never stamped. Wren's eyes are already burning, and the print swims when she blinks. She has perhaps an hour of proper reading left in her before the words stop meaning anything. "All right, Grandpa," she says under her breath, "where did you put it?"

choices.label: Read the water-stained logbook.
Go through the QSL cards.
Untie the ribbon round the envelopes.

nodes.body: She unties the ribbon round the envelopes, and they slide apart across her knees. Every one is addressed in his handwriting to the same place, Relay KX on the headland, and not one of them has a stamp. Wren draws the top letter out and unfolds it, soft as cloth along the creases. It is written to a man called Kell, and it begins: Kell, she may still be out there, so keep the channel open. Wren sits back on her heels. Her grandfather knew somebody at that dead station well enough to use his first name, and to write to him for years, and never to post a word. He was not listening to a stranger but rooting for a friend, across all that dark water, for longer than she has been alive.

choices.label: Read further down the page.

nodes.body: The letter goes on to use his full name, Kell Alder, the operator at the headland relay, and to plead with him, gently and stubbornly, not to give up on his own daughter. Reading it is like opening a drawer in somebody else's house. These are two old men's private sorrows, set down by one of them in careful ink and never posted, and Wren can think of only one reason for writing a letter and keeping it. He did not want it read. Under the top sheet the bundle is thirty envelopes thick. The ribbon lies across her knee where she dropped it, still holding the shape of its knot.

choices.label: Read on through the bundle.
Retie the ribbon and leave them unread.

nodes.body: She reads on through the bundle, one letter and then the next, and by the third her eyes are stinging. They are all written to the same man. Kell, they begin, and they go on to tell an operator named Alder, out at the headland relay, that somebody hears him every night, that his girl may yet be listening too, and that he is not to give up. Not one of them was ever stamped. Her grandfather wrote to that man for years and could not bring himself to post a word of it. Wren folds the top letter along its old creases and keeps it.

choices.label: Close the trunk.

nodes.body: She reties the ribbon exactly as she found it and lays the letters back in the trunk, unread, because some grief is not hers to open. It feels like the kind thing to do, and perhaps it is. A week later, hunting for something else, she lifts the bundle out again and turns it over. On the back of the last envelope, in pencil so faint that she has to tilt it to the light, her grandfather has left a line for whoever came after him: IF I AM GONE, TAKE THESE OUT TO KX BY HAND, BECAUSE HE NEEDS TO KNOW SOMEBODY HEARD. Wren carries them up to the attic and switches on the radio to find the man they belong to. There is only hiss. She sits for a long time with thirty letters in her lap and nowhere on earth to deliver them.

The water-stained logbook tracks the KX loop for years, in entry after entry, and it keeps circling back to one underlined line: ALDER STILL TRANSMITTING, WHY. Beside the third of these he has added a note in smaller writing, to say that the operator is a man named Alder, out at the headland relay, and that nobody at the club will talk about him. So he heard it too, night after night, and it nagged at him. The last page is dated the week he died. The handwriting is shakier there, but it is still his, and it asks only one thing: will anybody ever answer the poor man? Wren sits with the book open on her knees. He left that question unfinished, and it has landed in her lap.

choices.label: Take up the question he left.

nodes.body: The QSL cards spill across Wren's lap by the dozen. They are postcards from listeners up and down the coast, each one confirming that a signal was heard on such a night at such an hour. Most are cheerful, the radio version of a wave from a passing boat. One card is heavier than the rest, on thicker paper and in older ink, and it names a frequency and a call sign: KX ALDER, underlined twice in her grandfather's own hand. Beneath it the stack goes on and on, forty years deep and in no order at all. Her grandfather was not a man who kept forty years of anything by accident.

choices.label: Chase the card naming KX Alder.
Sort the whole stack by date.

nodes.body: She chases the heavier card through the rest of the stack and finds its twin, and then a third. All three name the same station, RELAY KX, HEADLAND, and the same operator, a man named Alder, and all three give a frequency that matches the loop to the last decimal. He checked it, and then he checked it again. Along the edge of the newest card he has penciled the number of nights he logged that signal, and the number runs to four figures. A coast of listeners heard this man for years and sent cheerful postcards about it. As far as Wren can tell from forty years of cards, not one of them ever picked up a microphone and answered him.

choices.label: Put the three cards together.

nodes.body: She sorts the whole stack by date, because that is how he would have done it, and the job takes her until three in the morning. Forty years of strangers go by under her hands: fishermen, lighthouse keepers, a nun in a convent two counties north. All of them heard the same stubborn signal, and all of them wrote to tell him so. The newest card is eleven years old and carries no call sign at all, only one line in a woman's looping hand: Heard KX again tonight, please do not tell him, M. Wren falls asleep with that card on her chest and wakes to her alarm with ink on her chin. Two days pass before that single initial means anything to her. By then the loop has gone quiet, and there is nobody left on the headland to tell.

The radio shed smells of solder and dust, as it always has. Her grandfather's tuning notes are pinned in careful ranks across one wall, hundreds of them, a lifetime of frequencies in his small square hand, and reading them all would take until morning. In the corner stands the steel filing cabinet where he kept his letters, with a padlock through its hasp and the key gone to wherever his keys went. A man does not padlock a drawer full of nothing. His long screwdriver is still lying on the bench, where he put it down.

choices.label: Read the pinned tuning notes.
Force the cabinet padlock with his screwdriver.

nodes.body: She reads the pinned tuning notes from the top row down, hundreds of them. It is the ninth row before one stops her. It is yellower than its neighbors, and circled twice in pencil pressed so hard that the paper has nearly torn: KX LOOP, HEADLAND RELAY, OPERATOR ALDER, DO NOT GIVE UP ON HIM. Under that, in ordinary writing, he has added that the operator Alder never answers, and that he means to keep trying anyway. Wren reads it three times. Her grandfather spent years trying to reach that man, quietly, the way he did everything, and he ran out of time before he managed it. The note has hung here ever since with its two hard circles, waiting for somebody to take it down.

choices.label: Unpin the note.

nodes.body: She forces the screwdriver through the padlock and leans on it with her whole weight, and the cabinet, which turns out not to be bolted to anything, comes over with a crash like a dropped piano. Wren only just gets out from under it. By the time her mother reaches the shed in a bathrobe, she is sitting in a drift of fallen notes with a bent screwdriver in her fist, and there is nothing useful to say. The shed is locked for the night, and so, very nearly, is she. One thing came loose in the fall, though. A slip of card had been wedged behind the top drawer, in his writing: KX, EVERY MIDNIGHT, TWO DOTS, NO REPLY YET. She reads it under her blanket by flashlight, wide awake, wondering what he was sending, and to whom, and why the answer was pinned to the wall she did not read.

Wren reads the name Alder once more, in handwriting she would know anywhere, and the house seems to go quiet around it. Her grandfather knew that somebody was out there on the headland, keeping that station alive long after it was supposed to be dead. He knew, and he listened, night after night, and for some reason he never told a soul. The loop is still running, faint and patient, as it has been all night. It is strange to think that he sat under that same sound for years with the same question she has now, and ran out of time to answer it. She slides what she has found inside her jacket and looks at the clock, which says it is not yet one.

choices.label: Fetch the bicycle from the garage.

nodes.body: The headland road is empty at this hour, and the wind off the water pushes at her front wheel all the way out. Her grandfather must have looked along this road a thousand times and, as far as she knows, never once driven it. The station gate is chained, but the fence beside it has pulled away from its post, and Wren has left her bicycle in the gorse and ducked through before she can think better of it. The place is not dark. A red lamp burns at the top of the mast, and in the low building at its foot one window is lit a warm yellow. She crosses the yard with her heart going like a fist on a door, and stops beside that window with her back against the wall.

choices.label: Look through the lit window.

nodes.body: She turns her head, slowly, and looks in. The room behind the glass is small and crowded and warm: a console of dials, two reels of tape turning on a machine the size of a suitcase, a chair pushed back from a desk, a mug with the steam still rising from it. A framed license hangs on the wall, close enough to read, made out to a man named Kell Alder of Station KX. Under it a shelf sags beneath a row of logbooks with a year inked on every spine, and Wren counts thirty before she runs out of shelf. So the loop is no machine left running by mistake. Alder is a person, the owner of that mug and that chair, and he has sat there every night for thirty years. Somewhere behind the building a door bangs, and a flashlight beam comes swinging along the fence toward her. She has a pencil stub, a scrap of paper, and perhaps one minute.

choices.label: Wedge a note in the door frame.
Back away before the flashlight finds her.

nodes.body: The note takes her ten seconds: she tears the scrap in half against her knee and writes on it in the dark, three words and an initial, with the pencil pressing through to her palm. It says I HEAR YOU, and under that a single W, and there is no time to decide whether leaving it is brave or stupid. She wedges the paper into the door frame at the height of a tall man's eyes and runs, bent double, back the way she came. From the far side of the fence she looks around once. The flashlight has stopped at the door, and it stays there, perfectly still, for a long time.

choices.label: Ride home.

nodes.body: She backs away from the glass before the flashlight can reach it, one slow step at a time, and then she turns and runs, bent double, the way she came. Behind her the beam sweeps over the wall where she was standing and finds nothing but wet brick, and nobody shouts. From the far side of the fence she looks around once, and sees a tall, stooped figure cross the lit window and sit down at the desk. He never knew that she was there. All the way home she cannot decide whether that feels like an escape or like hanging up on somebody.

choices.label: Ride home.

nodes.body: She sleeps for four hours and carries the name through school like a stone in her shoe. By late afternoon it is written on an index card and pinned to the corkboard over her desk, between a page of copied numbers and a map of the headland: KELL ALDER, KX. The county's own website gives the relay station a single line, which says that it was decommissioned thirty years ago and has no staff. Somebody forgot to tell the man at the desk. Wren says his name out loud to her empty bedroom, to hear what it sounds like, and it sounds like somebody she is going to have to meet.

choices.label: Sit down at the desk.

nodes.body: A name is not an answer, only the place where an answer might start. On her corkboard the numbers wait in their columns. Kell Alder sends them out every night, and nobody goes to that much trouble over numbers that mean nothing. Then there is the man himself. This is a small town, and a person does not sit alone on a headland for thirty years without somebody noticing, or remembering, or minding. Wren has a few hours of the evening left and a head that keeps drifting back to that steaming mug. Whatever he is saying, he was saying it a minute before she looked in, and he will be saying it again tonight.

choices.label: Crack the coded numbers.
Ask the town about Kell Alder.

nodes.body: She copies the numbers out in full across a fresh page and stares at them until they begin to swim. Old operators loved a book cipher, in which every group points to a page and a line in some book that both ends own. Her grandfather's logbook lies by her elbow, fetched down from the cedar trunk in the attic, and tucked inside its back cover is the one book every operator on this coast once owned: the club's printed station register. But the groups arrive on a strict beat, and when she taps her pencil along with the recording, the beat is not quite steady. It might not be writing at all. It might be time, counted out loud. Her stopwatch is in the desk drawer, the logbook is under her hand, and her eyes will last for one long job tonight.

choices.label: Try the station register as a book cipher.
Time the groups with the stopwatch.

nodes.body: Wren opens the station register and treats every group of numbers as a page and a line, the way a book cipher works, counting her way down to a word. Fragments arrive almost at once: HOLDING, and ANSWER, and a single letter, M, which turns up too often to be an accident. Then the method stalls. One cluster near the end of the string comes out as nonsense however she counts it, and she counts it four different ways. Perhaps she has slipped by a page somewhere in the register. Perhaps that cluster was never keyed to the register at all. On the shelf above the desk sits the only other book of his that is underlined half as heavily, its spine cracked white with use.

choices.label: Go back through the register key, page by page.
Take down the underlined book from the shelf.

nodes.body: The register key holds after all, because she was only one page off, and once she shifts it every group drops into place like a bolt sliding home. The numbers make one plain sentence: STILL HOLDING THE CHANNEL OPEN FOR M. Wren reads it aloud to the empty room and has to stop and swallow before she can go on. The last group is not a word at all but a figure, and when she checks tonight's copy against last night's, the figure is smaller. Whatever else this broadcast is, part of it is a count, and the count is going down.

choices.label: Take the sentence up to the radio.

nodes.body: The underlined book from the shelf turns out to be a battered tide table, its pages soft and rippled from years of salt air. Against that key the stubborn cluster gives way at once, and what it gives her is not a word but a date and an hour. Wren sits back, pleased with herself, and then tries the same key on the rest of the string, where it produces pure rubbish, line after line of it. So she is holding one clean fact wrapped in a wall of noise. A proper codebreaker would not trust a single fragment until the whole message came out to match it. Her grandfather said so often, generally while getting something wrong.

choices.label: Trust the one date and hour.
Run the tide table against the whole string.

nodes.body: One recovered date is not much, but Wren decides to trust it, and she writes it out at the top of a clean page. It is today's date, and beside it sits an hour: 23:40. She runs the tide-table key through the same cluster twice more and gets the identical answer both times. So the numbers are not only a message, because somewhere inside them is a clock, and the clock is set for tonight, twenty minutes before midnight. She looks at her watch and finds that it is not yet eight.

choices.label: Go up and listen for the clock in it.

nodes.body: She runs the tide table against the whole string, group by group, and then backwards, and then with the columns swapped, filling page after page with rubbish. It becomes a matter of pride. Somewhere after the fourth notebook she stops looking at the clock, and when she finally straightens her back, the house is silent and it is ten past one in the morning. She climbs to the attic to hear the numbers once more before bed, and there are no numbers, only a soft clean hiss. Wren goes slowly back down to her desk. The one fragment the tide table ever gave her is still there at the top of the first page, circled: today's date, and an hour, 23:40. It was never part of a longer message. It was the whole message, and she spent it doing sums.

Wren times the groups with the stopwatch in one hand and a notebook balanced on her knee, logging the gap between one cycle of the loop and the next. It takes eleven cycles before she believes what the column of figures is telling her. The gaps are shrinking. Each cycle comes round a little sooner than the one before, by an amount far too regular to be a tired machine. Something is closing in on something. A dozen more cycles would give her a curve she could trust to the minute. The calendar hangs right there on the wall, though, and the rough figures she already has would fit onto it now, if she is willing to be a little wrong.

choices.label: Keep timing the shrinking gaps.
Lay the rough figures on the calendar.

nodes.body: She keeps timing the loop, cycle after cycle, until the stopwatch has pressed a red dent into her palm. On graph paper the shrinking intervals make a clean curve, and a curve can be followed, so she lays her ruler along it and draws the line down to where it touches zero. It does not land on next month, or even next week. It lands on tonight, a little before midnight. Wren puts the pencil down very carefully, as though the page might go off in her hands. Whatever this loop is, it was never going to run forever: it is counting down, and it is nearly finished.

choices.label: Take the graph up to the radio.

nodes.body: Laid on the calendar, the rough figures close in on a single square, and the square is today. Wren stares at it. That is the sort of answer a tired person would find at this hour, whether it was there or not. People see faces in clouds and hear their own names in running water, and she has been listening to static for a week with nobody to tell her when to stop. Her figures are rough, and her method is one she invented an hour ago. A scientist would test that method on something she knew for certain was empty, to see whether it found a date in there as well.

choices.label: Trust the square and circle the date.
Test the method on plain static first.

nodes.body: Wren commits to it: she circles the date twice, hard enough that the pencil nearly goes through the paper, and only then lets herself read it properly. It is today. The intervals are closing on tonight like a hand closing, and threaded through every cycle is that one stubborn letter, M. So the loop is a countdown, and it ends tonight, whether or not a single soul is listening when it does. She looks at the circled square on the calendar, and then up at the ceiling, where the attic is.

choices.label: Climb up to the radio.

nodes.body: She tests the method on plain static, ten minutes of empty hiss from the far end of the dial, timed and logged exactly like the loop. The static gives her a date as well. It gives her the fourteenth of March, with great confidence, and Wren laughs out loud and drops the calendar in the bin. She does her homework and brushes her teeth, and she is spitting into the sink at twenty to midnight when the sound from the attic changes. The numbers have stopped. A man's voice, old and tired, says a single name, and after that there is nothing at all. Static does not say goodbye to anyone. Wren fishes the calendar back out of the bin with toothpaste still on her chin, and the square she would not circle is today.

Asking a town about one of its own turns out to mean choosing whom to ask. The county library keeps the local paper on microfilm, a hundred years of it in gray steel drawers, and the reading room stays open until seven. Print does not gossip, and it does not look at you while you read it. Down at the marina, old Mrs. Okafor has been mending nets within sight of that headland since before the relay was built, and people say she remembers everything and repeats almost none of it. Wren has never said more to her than hello. She wheels her bicycle out of the garage, and at the end of the road the library lies to the left and the harbor to the right.

choices.label: Search the library microfilm.
Ask Mrs. Okafor at the marina.

nodes.body: The library microfilm reader whirs and clicks, and decades of front pages slide past under the glass faster than Wren can read them. She stops at a photograph of the relay station with a crowd outside it, under a headline about the county closing it down. Beside the story is a second picture, of one man standing apart from all the others with his hands in his pockets. The article runs on for three long columns of small gray print. Behind her the librarian is stacking chairs. "Ten minutes, love," he calls, "and that machine wants five of them to cool down before I can put its cover on." There are four more reels in the box at her elbow, and Wren has not opened one of them.

choices.label: Read the article through, slowly.
Photograph every page she can reach.

nodes.body: She reads the article through slowly, with a finger under the lines, while the chairs go up on the tables behind her. The man standing apart is Kell Alder, the relay's senior operator. He is the only one of nine staff who refused the transfer inland. Asked why, he gave the reporter a single sentence, which the reporter plainly took for a joke: somebody has to keep the channel open. The paper printed it under his picture as a caption. That was thirty years ago this spring, and the piece is written in the tone people use about a man who will see sense in a week or two. Wren copies the sentence onto the back of her hand, because her notebook is at the bottom of her bag.

choices.label: Ride home before dark.

nodes.body: She photographs every page she can reach, reel after reel, while the librarian jingles his keys beside the door. At home she spreads the pictures across her screen, and most of them are useless: council meetings, a flower show, a column of tide times. Two are not. The first is a caption under a man's picture, which reads K. Alder, senior operator, the one who would not go. The second is a letter to the editor from eleven years later, signed only by a neighbor, complaining that the old relay still hums at night and that somebody ought to tell that poor man nobody is listening. In the margin of the microfilm an earlier reader has written three words in pencil: are you sure?

choices.label: Go up to the attic.

nodes.body: Mrs. Okafor is sitting on a stool outside the net loft with a torn net across her knees, and she does not look up when Wren asks about a man named Alder. "Sit," she says, nodding at an upturned crate, and for a while there is only the needle going in and out. "In thirty years nobody under fifty has asked me about Kell," she says at last, "so before I say one word, you will tell me why you want to know." Her eyes come up then, sharp as fishhooks. The truth is an attic, a dead man's radio, and a voice reading numbers in the night, and said out loud at five in the afternoon it is going to sound insane, which a school project would not. Wren's mouth has gone dry.

choices.label: Tell her the truth about the attic radio.
Say it is for a school project.

nodes.body: Wren tells her the truth about the attic radio, all of it, badly, and the old woman's needle slows and then stops. "So somebody finally listened," she says. "I have pinned a card to the pier board every month for thirty years, telling people that loop is real, and you are the first who ever came." After that she tells it plainly: Kell Alder had a daughter, and one winter the two of them had a quarrel that the whole harbor could hear, and the girl took the morning bus and never wrote. He swore in front of witnesses that he would keep a channel open until she answered. "Her name is his to say, not mine," Mrs. Okafor says, "but if that loop of his ever looks like stopping, child, you ring the marina, day or night."

choices.label: Ride home with it.

nodes.body: "It's for a school project," Wren says, "on local history." The old woman looks at her for a long moment and then bends to her net again. "Then it will keep until daylight, and you can go home to your supper and your bed," she says, not unkindly, "because I do not hand a man's grief to a school project." Wren has got as far as her bicycle when Mrs. Okafor calls after her, without turning her head. "You have been listening to that voice reading the numbers, I can see that much, so ask yourself why a man would keep a girl's voice on the air for thirty years. When you are ready to tell me the truth, child, you know where I sit." The harbor lights are coming on, and Wren stands holding her handlebars, with her face burning and a new question that is worse than the old one.

That night Wren climbs the attic ladder with her head full, and sits down in front of the radio as if it were a person she had come to interview. The loop begins the way it always does, with two long tones that she has heard all week and taken for the machine clearing its throat. Tonight she checks them against the old Morse chart her grandfather taped inside the lid, where dash, dash is a single letter: M. Then come the numbers in that flat, careful voice, and then the slow tone stepping down and down. After the tone, before everything starts over, there is a gap of four seconds, nothing but open air, which she has never noticed because nothing happens in it. That is the point of it. He names someone, he says his piece, and then he stops and listens for an answer. "Oh," Wren says out loud, "you're waiting."

choices.label: Lean close and listen to the gap again.
Press his headset tight and listen under the voice.

nodes.body: She presses the cracked leather pads tight against her ears, the way he used to, and listens under the voice instead of to it. Between one number and the next, faint as a watermark, an older recording is bleeding through the tape, and in it a man says, "Again, and slower this time." There is a sigh, and then a girl answers him, bored and fond at once: "Dad, I am going slow." The next number arrives flat and careful, in the same voice made patient. Wren sits very still, because the voice reading the numbers belongs to a girl not much older than she is, and that girl called the man at that station Dad.

choices.label: Write down what the tape gave up.

nodes.body: She pulls her notebook over and does what her grandfather would have done, which is to log it: the time, the frequency, and the note the slow tone starts on. Last night the tone began at the top of its scale, but tonight it begins four steps lower, and the gap at the end is a full second shorter. She turns back through the pages for the week and finds the same thing every night, a little lower and a little less. A loop that has asked one question for years ought to sound the same each time it asks. This one is running out of room.

choices.label: Underline it twice.

nodes.body: Two questions sit on the page under her pencil. The first is a name: who is M, that a man would call for so long and never hang up? The second is a clock: what is the count running down to, now that it has stopped starting over from the top? Downstairs the kitchen clock strikes nine, and the loop comes round again with its two tones, its numbers, its falling note, and its held breath of silence. Each question is a night's work, and Wren is beginning to suspect that she does not have two nights.

choices.label: Go after the name behind the M.
Go after the clock and what it runs down to.

nodes.body: A name has to start somewhere, and the loop itself gives her only a single letter. An M can be a person, since operators have families, and families leave records behind them: births, school photographs, a line in the county register. An M can just as easily be a place. Her grandfather's marine chart of the headland lies rolled on the desk, its margins crowded with letters that each stand for a mooring or a marker. Men keep watch over places too, and keep lights burning for boats that never came in. Wren looks from her laptop to the rolled chart and back again.

choices.label: Search the Alder family records for an M.
Unroll the chart and hunt for an M on it.

nodes.body: The Alder family takes up very little room in the county records, and Wren has all of it on one screen inside ten minutes. Kell Alder had one child, his daughter Marin. She was born in the cottage hospital, and she vanished from every local register thirty years ago, with no forwarding address. Wren says the name under her breath, and it fits those two long tones like a key in a lock. The same records list one other Alder who never left: his sister, still living three streets from the harbor, with a telephone number that has not changed since before Wren was born. It is twenty minutes to ten at night. One of them has dropped out of the paperwork, and the other is very probably asleep.

choices.label: Hunt for Marin herself online.
Telephone his sister, late as it is.

nodes.body: Marin Alder left almost no trail to hunt along, and what there is Wren pieces together from scraps. She finds a school prize for reading aloud, a name on a ferry crew list, and a wedding notice two counties away. One old thread on a radio hobby forum mentions her directly. Kell's girl used to read the station numbers for him, somebody wrote, lovely clear voice, and then there was a row and she went, and he has been calling her home ever since. Wren reads that line until it blurs. So M is Marin, the loop is an apology, and the person it is meant for has spent thirty years somewhere it cannot reach her.

choices.label: Shut the laptop.

nodes.body: His sister answers the telephone on the ninth ring, and Wren apologizes three times before she manages to explain why she is calling. There is a long silence on the line. "You can hear it," the woman says at last, and her voice has cracked right down the middle. "I stopped being able to listen years ago, and I am ashamed of that. M is Marin, his girl, my niece, and the two of them had one terrible quarrel that neither would bend on." She gives Wren the last address she has, in a town two ridges west, where nobody has answered a card in years. "If you find a way to reach her," she says, "do it soon, because he is not a young man, and that station is older than he is."

choices.label: Write the address down.

nodes.body: Unrolled and pinned flat under four coffee mugs, the chart shows every rock and channel around the headland, and Wren hunts across it with a fingertip. She finds the M in her grandfather's own pencil, a small neat letter beside a mooring just inside the breakwater, ringed twice. There is no boat's name beside it and no depth, only the letter and a date thirty years old. Something happened at that spot. The breakwater is a fifteen-minute ride away, the tide is on the turn, and rain has begun to tap at the window. Under the lamp the pencil ring looks very small. The rest of the chart is crowded with other letters she has not read yet, dozens of them, any one of which might matter more.

choices.label: Ride out to the mooring by the breakwater.
Stay in and work through the rest of the chart.

nodes.body: The mooring itself lies under black water, but its old buoy has been hauled up and chained to the harbor wall above it, and Wren finds it with her flashlight on the second pass. Somebody has screwed a small brass plate to the rusted iron. The plate carries the name Marin, and a date, and beneath the date a line so worn that she has to read it with her fingertips: HER MOORING IS KEPT. Nobody keeps a mooring for the dead. People keep one for a boat that is expected back. Wren stands in the wind with her hand on the cold brass, understanding that M was never a place, only a place held open for a person.

choices.label: Ride home against the wind.

nodes.body: She stays in and works through the rest of the chart, letter by letter, while the rain gets louder on the glass. There are forty-one marks in her grandfather's pencil. Most are moorings, three are wrecks, and one, absurdly, is the place where he once lost a good hat. Each of them sends her to the tide book, the harbor register, or the back of the logbook, and each of them brings her round again to that small ringed M beside the breakwater. She is on her second lap when the radio behind her says something about one hour, and she tells it to hush. She is on her third when it stops reading numbers. A man's voice says a name, once, like somebody setting down a thing he has carried too far, and then the channel is empty. Her finger is resting on the only mark he ever ringed twice.

A clock can be read in two ways, and Wren has both of them within reach. The first is plain arithmetic: she has a week of logged starting notes, and a falling line can be followed down to the minute it hits bottom. The second is a hunch that refuses to leave her alone, because old operators timed everything by the sea. This year's tide table hangs on its nail by the window, and the evening forecast has been muttering about the headland all day. She taps the pencil against her teeth while, outside, the wind begins to lean on the house.

choices.label: Follow the falling line down to zero.
Check the count against the tide table and the forecast.

nodes.body: She follows the falling line down the page with a ruler, and it touches zero at twenty minutes to midnight, tonight. Wren works it three times, hoping to be wrong, and gets the same minute each time. A countdown has to be counting toward something, though, and arithmetic cannot tell her what. The county archive has two documents on the relay, and she has printed both. One is a maintenance sheet, three pages of dull figures about the station's power cell. The other is a smudged photocopy of its operating schedule, a typed grid on which somebody has crossed out a single date and moved it later, more than once. It is five past ten, and she reads slowly when she is frightened.

choices.label: Read through the maintenance sheet.
Read through the operating schedule.

nodes.body: The maintenance sheet is three pages of dull figures, and its last line makes Wren go cold. The relay runs on a single sealed power cell, installed the year the county walked away and never replaced, because nobody was left to sign for a new one. Its rated life ended eleven years ago, and every night since has been borrowed. She lays the cell's decay curve over her own falling line, and the two meet at the same minute. So that is what the count is. Kell Alder has not put a timer on his broadcast. He has measured how long his station has left to live, to the minute, and he is reading the answer out loud.

choices.label: Look at the clock.

nodes.body: The operating schedule is a typed grid of hours, thirty years of them identical, and Wren nearly misses the one line that is different. Under the heading FINAL somebody has typed: PLAY TAPE 2, THEN ERASE ALL. The date beside it has been crossed out and moved later three times, in three different inks, as if the operator kept finding reasons to wait. The last date has not been crossed out. It is today's, and the hour is twenty to midnight. So the count does not only stop. When it reaches zero the station will say one last thing, once, to whoever happens to be listening, and then it will wipe itself clean.

choices.label: Look at the clock.

nodes.body: The tide table and the forecast agree with each other, and with the count, a great deal too well. High water tonight is a spring tide, the biggest of the month, and it tops out at eighteen minutes to midnight. The forecast carries a gale warning for the headland from eleven o'clock. Wren has seen what a spring tide does to the low road under the headland on a calm day, and with a gale behind it the sea will be standing in the station yard. She could be wrong, of course. She is a kid with a pencil line and a column of figures, and it is past ten at night. Her grandfather used to say that the sea was the only clock on this coast that never needed winding.

choices.label: Trust the tide table and act on it tonight.
Check the figures again in daylight.

nodes.body: She trusts the tide table, because her grandfather did, and because the sea has never been late. That makes tonight simple and terrible. At twenty to midnight the biggest tide of the month will be standing in that station yard with a gale behind it, and whatever is counting down out there will be drowned at the very minute it reaches zero. Perhaps that is no coincidence. A man who has timed everything by the sea for thirty years would know when it was coming for him. Wren pulls her waterproof jacket off the back of the door and lays it across the desk, where she cannot forget it.

choices.label: Look at the clock.

nodes.body: She decides to check the figures again in daylight. A careful person does not ring strangers at ten at night on the strength of a pencil line. She sets her alarm for six, folds the tide table neatly on top of her notebook, and sleeps the deep sleep of somebody who has behaved sensibly. At six the figures are exactly what they were. The sea came in at eighteen minutes to midnight, to the minute, with a gale behind it, and the attic radio is giving out nothing but hiss. On the local news a reporter in a yellow coat is standing in front of the headland. The tide knocked out the power at the old relay station, she explains, and nobody has broadcast from there in thirty years. Wren knows one thing that the reporter does not.

At twenty minutes to eleven the numbers stop in the middle of a group, which in a week of listening they have never done, and Wren's head comes up as if somebody had spoken her name. There is a click, a wash of tape hiss, and then a man's voice, old and close to the microphone, recorded on some other night for use on this one. "KX, KX, this is your father, Marin," it says. "The cell will not carry another schedule, so this is the last one, and it has one hour left to run. I will say my piece at the end of it, and after that I am going to let you be." The tape clicks off, and the two long tones come back, and the numbers, and the falling note, exactly as before. But M is his daughter Marin, the hour is real, and this time the count will not start over.

choices.label: Keep listening.
Keep listening after the tape clicks off.

nodes.body: She keeps listening after the tape clicks off, and so she hears what comes next, in the gap where there has never been anything at all. The tape clicks on again, and the old voice goes on more slowly, as if he were reading the words off a scrap of paper held up to the lamp. "One more thing, for the W who left three words in my door: I walked the fence twice looking for you, and I have carried that paper in my shirt pocket ever since. I wanted you to know that one answer, even from a stranger, was worth every one of the thirty years. That is all, KX clear." Wren has both hands pressed over her mouth. He recorded that for her, and then he went back to counting down.

choices.label: Get up from the radio.

nodes.body: Rain arrives against the attic window all at once, like a handful of gravel, and Wren is on her feet without having decided to stand. One hour is nothing. One hour is the ride out to the headland in good weather, and this is not good weather: a gale is already leaning on the roof, and the streetlight at the end of the road is swinging on its wire. She thinks of that small warm room behind the glass, with its mug and its chair and its thirty logbooks. She thinks of a man who can measure the death of his own station to the minute. He has decided to spend its last hour talking to someone who left.

choices.label: Look at her watch.

nodes.body: Her watch says nineteen minutes to eleven, which leaves fifty-nine, and she spends the first of them standing perfectly still. A bicycle in the garage, her grandfather's transmitter under its dust sheet, a telephone on the desk: that is everything she has to throw at the relay station from here. Nobody else knows. That is the part she cannot get past. If she does nothing, nothing will happen, and it will happen at twenty to midnight exactly, to an old man beside a failing cell and a daughter who may not be listening. Whatever she does instead, she will be doing it for the first time, in a gale, with no one to ask.

choices.label: Ride for the relay station.
Uncover Grandpa's transmitter.
Pick up the telephone and wake someone.

nodes.body: She rides for the relay station with her head down and the rain coming at her sideways, and the cliff road takes fifty of her minutes and most of her legs. The gate is chained, and beyond it the mast lamp blinks in time with the loop, while under the mast the yard has turned to a sheet of black water, ruffled by the wind. The fence beside the gate is head high and rattling. To her left the service road curves away round the back of the compound, in the shelter of the buildings, toward a door she cannot see from here. Her watch says nine minutes. A gust takes the bicycle out of her hands and lays it flat in the gorse.

choices.label: Climb the fence into the yard.
Take the service road round to the back.

nodes.body: She climbs the fence into the yard in one scrambling, graceless heave, and drops into water that comes over her ankles and knocks the breath out of her. Thirty yards away, across the open yard, a door stands ajar with warm light spilling out of it. The gale has those thirty yards to itself. It comes over the sea wall in solid gusts, carrying spray, and when Wren stands up straight it shoves her a full step sideways. Along the left side of the yard runs a row of low sheds, and the water in their shelter lies flat and still. That way round is three times as far, and her watch says five minutes.

choices.label: Run straight across the open yard.
Work round behind the row of sheds.

nodes.body: She runs straight across the open yard with the gale trying to peel her off the concrete, and the door gives under her shoulder. Inside is a control room that is all dials and switches, warm as a kitchen and completely empty. A mug still steams beside the microphone. Through the far window a flashlight jerks about at the foot of the mast, where somebody is fighting a loose cable in the storm. At the center of the console, red numbers count down, and a strip of tape underneath them reads, in neat capitals: AFTER LAST SEND, ERASE. Next to the tape sits a guarded switch marked HOLD. An address book lies open beside the telephone, with one number circled so many times that the paper shines. Under the desk the power cell gutters in its rusted housing, and every time it dips, the red numbers dim along with it. "Okay," Wren tells the empty room, "one thing at a time."

choices.label: Go to the microphone and answer the signal.
Try to steady the dying power cell.

nodes.body: The red numbers drop under two minutes while Wren stands at the microphone with her mouth open and nothing in it. What would she even say to him? Her eyes go back to the strip of tape, AFTER LAST SEND, ERASE, and at last she understands the plan: he means to say it once, and then wipe thirty years of tape clean behind him. The telephone on the desk has a patch cord running straight into the console. If she dials the circled number, his last message will play down the line to the one person it was always meant for, and the tape will erase itself afterward, as promised. The HOLD switch under its little guard would stop the sending and the erasing both. The red numbers say one minute and forty seconds, and the mug beside her has not even stopped steaming.

choices.label: Dial the circled number and let his message play.
Throw the HOLD switch and save the tapes.

nodes.body: She dials the circled number with the red numbers falling through their last minute, and patches the line into the console as the count reaches zero. Somewhere west of here a telephone rings in a dark kitchen, and a woman has just said hello when the reels turn over and her father's voice fills the wire. "Marin, I kept your voice on the air so that you would always know the way home. I am sorry, and I have been sorry for thirty years." The tape runs out and begins, as promised, to erase itself. Nobody on the line speaks. Then the yard door bangs open behind Wren, and an old man stands there with the storm coming in round him, and she holds the handset out to him at the full length of its cord. "It's for you," she says.

She throws the HOLD switch with eleven seconds showing, and the red numbers stop as if they had hit a wall. Nothing is sent, and nothing is erased, and on the big machine the reels coast to a standstill, thirty years of them, every night he ever logged and every word he could not say to her face. Wren lets out a breath she seems to have been holding since the attic. The yard door bangs open, and an old man stands dripping on the mat with a flashlight in his fist, staring from the frozen count to the girl beside it. "I could not let you wipe it," she says, "because she might want to hear all of it, and not just the end." He looks at her for a long time, and then he hangs up his coat, like a man who has decided to stay.

The power cell is a corroded brick bolted under the desk, humming unevenly against her palm and warm in all the wrong places. Its needle twitches near the bottom of the dial. Beside it two bare terminals stick up, where a second cell was meant to ride and never has, and a fresh battery clipped across them would carry the station for hours. Without one there is only this cell and her own two hands, pressing its loose connector tight and hoping. Above her the red numbers dim, catch, and dim again. "Don't," she whispers to the cell, "not yet, please, not yet."

choices.label: Splice in Grandpa's spare battery.
Nurse the dying cell by hand.
Leave the cell and run back to the microphone.

nodes.body: She drags the spare battery out of the bottom of her pack, rag and all, and the label in his square capitals makes her throat go tight: JUST IN CASE. Two clips go on, red to red and black to black, the way he showed her on a camping lantern when she was nine. The needle swings up, the lamps stop flickering, and the red numbers burn steady for the first time tonight. They are still counting, but the station will not die underneath them now, not for hours. That changes everything on this desk: the telephone with the radio club's night number taped to it, the guarded HOLD switch, the circled number in the address book. Hours are enough to do this properly. They might even be enough to do more than one thing.

choices.label: Phone the radio club and hand it on.
Throw the HOLD switch, then dial the circled number.

nodes.body: The radio club's night operator picks up the phone on the fourth ring, and Wren gives it to him straight: relay KX, a cell about to die, a spare battery holding it up, and a last message on a timer. "Hold on," he says, suddenly wide awake, "do you mean Kell Alder's KX?" By the time the gale has blown itself out, there are three trucks at the gate and a generator humming in the yard. Somebody has thrown the HOLD switch. Somebody else is on the telephone to a town two ridges west. The old man they fetch in from the mast stands dripping in his own doorway, staring at a room full of people who came because of him. On the console the red numbers have stopped, and thirty years of waiting belong to more than one person now.

The HOLD switch goes over with a clunk, and the red numbers freeze at forty-one seconds, with nothing sent and nothing erased and thirty years of tape safe on its reels. Then Wren picks up the telephone and dials the circled number with a finger that will not stay still. On the fourth ring a woman answers, wary and half asleep, and Wren gets the words out in one breath: "Is this Marin Alder? Please don't hang up, because I'm standing in your father's station, and he recorded something for you." She holds the handset to the speaker and starts the tape by hand, and his voice fills the little room. Behind her the yard door bangs open, and an old man stands there with rain running off him and a flashlight in his fist, listening to his daughter say, "Dad? Dad, are you there?"

She nurses the dying cell by hand, holding its loose connector tight, and for a while it works: the needle steadies, and the red numbers run all the way down to zero. There is a click, a hiss of tape, and then an old man's voice says, as close as a hand on her shoulder, "Marin." The cell dies under her fingers on that one word and takes the room with it, lamps and dials and voice together. She thumbed her phone to record as she ran in from the yard, so that single word, at least, has been saved in her jacket pocket. Kneeling in the dark, Wren thinks about two bare terminals, and about a spare battery wrapped in a rag on an attic shelf. JUST IN CASE, the label said, and this was the case.

She works her way round behind the row of sheds, where the wind cannot reach her, and it is exactly as far as it looked. The last shed ends ten yards short of the door. Wren is waiting there for a lull, with her back against the wet boards, when the mast lamp above her blinks twice and goes out. By the time she gets inside, the reels on the big machine are spinning backwards with a rising whine, wiping themselves clean, and the console is dark. On the desk, beside a mug that is still warm, lies an open address book with one telephone number circled until the paper shines. She is one minute too late to dial it. She stands holding the book in both hands, thinking that the straight way across was only thirty yards.

The service road is the long way round, but the buildings break the wind, and Wren runs the length of it with one hand on the wall. At the back of the station a lamp is burning behind a small square window. Through the glass she can see a console, a pair of turning reels, and an old man hunched over them with a heavy headset clamped on his ears and his back to her. Beside the window is a steel door. She tries the handle and finds it bolted on the inside. Rain sheets off the eave onto her shoulders. Six minutes are left, and the only other person awake on this headland is ten feet away behind a wall, listening to something else.

choices.label: Rap on the window glass.
Hammer on the steel door and shout.

nodes.body: She raps on the window glass with her knuckles and then with the flat of her hand, and the old man turns round. For a moment they stare at each other through the rain, and then he unbolts the door, and she is inside, dripping on his floor and saying all of it at once: the attic, the numbers, the two long tones, the hour. "You heard the schedule," Kell Alder says slowly, as if the words were in another language. He looks at the turning reels and back at her. "For thirty years I have put that out for one person, and she has never come, because she is not listening, child, and I stopped pretending that she was a long time ago. Tonight I am only saying goodbye." The red numbers behind him read four minutes.

choices.label: Admit that nobody can promise Marin is listening.
