Promise him that Marin is listening tonight.
Tell him the note in his door was hers.

nodes.body: "I can't promise you she's listening," Wren says, and the truth of it comes out steadier than she expected. "Nobody could, but you were sure that nobody was listening at all, and I was, from an attic eight miles away. So you don't know who else is out there, and neither do I." Kell Alder looks at her for a long moment. Then he stops the reels with his own hand, pulls the microphone toward him, and speaks into it live, for the first time in thirty years, with nothing recorded between him and the dark. "Marin, this is your father, and I am still here, I am still sorry, and I am listening." Two ridges west, a woman who never quite stopped tuning in picks up a handset with both hands and says, "Dad?"

"She's listening tonight, I promise," Wren says, and she watches the words land wrong. Kell Alder's face closes like a door. "People promised me that for ten years," he says, gently enough, "the harbormaster, the minister, my own sister, and none of them knew, any more than you do. If you had told me that you did not know, child, I might have believed the rest." He turns back to the console, and at twenty to midnight the tape plays his goodbye into an empty sky and wipes itself clean, as he planned. He does not ask her to leave. He fills a second mug from the flask and sets it on the desk in front of her, and the two of them sit in the hiss of a channel that is finally, properly closed.

"The note in your door was mine," Wren says, "the three words and the W." Kell Alder goes very still, and then he takes a folded scrap of paper out of his shirt pocket, already worn soft at the creases, and looks from it to her. "Whose attic did you hear me from?" he asks, and when she gives him the name Callahan, he laughs, one short astonished bark. "Two dots, every midnight, for twenty years, and I took it for a fault in the set," he says. "Your grandfather was answering me the whole time, and I was too deaf to know it." He stops the reels with his hand and pulls the microphone over, and his voice is not steady, but it is live: "Marin, this is your father, and it seems that people have been listening all along, so I am asking whether you are too." The speaker hisses for a long moment. Then, from somewhere far to the west, it gives back two soft clicks, and a woman's voice says, "I'm here, Dad, and I think I always was."

She hammers on the steel door with both fists and shouts his name until her voice cracks, and the gale takes every sound and throws it out to sea. Through the little window she can see him, six steps along the wall, hunched in his headset with his back to her, and he never turns. At twenty to midnight the reels stop and start again, and a voice she knows from the tape an hour ago comes faintly through the steel: "Marin, I kept your voice on the air so that you would always know the way home." Then the lamp goes out, and Wren stands with her forehead against the cold door, thinking about the window. It was glass. He was facing the other way, but it was glass, and it was only six steps along the wall.

ending.title: On the Wrong Side of the Door

nodes.body: She pulls the dust sheet off her grandfather's transmitter, and the smell of warm dust and old varnish comes up to meet her. He never let her key it, not once, because a transmitter needs a license and a license needs an exam. But she watched him do it for years: main switch, warm the valves, tune for the dip, and keep one eye on the needle. On the wall above the set his club card is still pinned, with the county radio net's emergency line printed across the bottom in red. A dozen licensed operators could put a message across three counties in the time it takes her to find the right band. That is, if any of them is awake, and if they will listen to a girl.

choices.label: Switch the transmitter on and send it herself.
Ring the radio net's emergency line.

nodes.body: She switches the transmitter on, and it comes up slowly, the valves glowing orange one by one, with a hum she has known all her life. Her hands remember more than she expected. She patches the receiver's output across, so that Alder's loop will go straight back out on her grandfather's old frequency with her own voice over the top of it. The needle sits at a quarter of its scale, beside a pencil mark, which is where he always kept it. A quarter will reach the next county on a good night. Marin Alder could be anywhere, and tonight is not a good night. The power knob turns a long way past that pencil mark, into a red band he never let it touch.

choices.label: Send at his pencil mark and call for Marin.
Turn the power up into the red band.

nodes.body: She sends at his pencil mark, steady and patient, with Marin's name riding out over the loop every thirty seconds, and for a long time nothing comes back but hiss. Her watch says twenty minutes, and then twelve. Then the receiver's needle twitches. Somebody out there has pressed a key and let it go again without a word, a bare carrier, there and gone, and then there again for a little longer. It might be a person who cannot make herself speak. It might just as easily be a trawler skipper wondering who is cluttering up his band. Downstairs the telephone has started ringing, and by the sound of it, it does not mean to stop.

choices.label: Speak to the silent carrier.
Run down and answer the telephone.

nodes.body: "This is for the station sending a carrier," Wren says into the microphone, as gently as she can. "You don't have to say anything, because I'm nobody, I'm only the one who heard him, but if you are Marin, key twice." The hiss goes on. Then the needle jumps, and jumps again, and a woman's voice comes up out of the static, older than the one that reads the numbers but with the very same careful vowels, so that there is no mistaking whose voice the loop has been keeping. "Who is this, and why is my name on the air?" Wren tells her in one breath: the relay, the cell, the last hour, a father who has kept her voice on a loop for thirty years. "He kept it," the woman says, and it is not a question. Wren turns the receiver up as loud as it will go, holds the microphone against it, and lets the two of them have the channel.

She runs down and answers the telephone, and it is a woman from two streets over who has had her kitchen radio on all evening. "Is that the Callahan house? I thought so, because I knew that old frequency. I do not know who Marin Alder is, dear, but I have just rung my brother, who is net controller for the whole county, and he says to keep sending." By the time Wren is back at the microphone there are stations answering her from three directions. None of them is Marin. But the message is moving now from one set to the next, like a lit match along a row of candles, further than her grandfather's transmitter could ever throw it. At twenty to midnight the loop falls silent on the headland, and all down the coast strangers are still saying her name.

She turns the power up into the red band, and for ten glorious seconds the needle stands at the top of its scale while her voice goes out across the dark coast: "Marin Alder, this is a message from KX, please listen." Then something inside the set says pop, quite gently. A thread of blue smoke rises from the back of the cabinet, the orange valves fade one by one, and the attic fills with the smell of scorched varnish. Wren sits in the dark with her hand still on the knob. Downstairs the telephone begins to ring, and it is a woman from two streets over, who heard ten seconds of a girl's voice on her kitchen radio and wants to know whether the rest of the message is coming. The rest is not coming. He kept that needle at the pencil mark for forty years, and he was not being timid.

She rings the radio net's emergency line, and a recorded voice answers on the second ring. It belongs to a man who sounds as if he has read these words into a machine many times before. "County radio net. If life or property is in danger at this moment, press one, and you will be put through to the duty controller at his home. For everything else, leave a message after the tone, and it will be heard at six tomorrow morning." Wren's thumb hovers over the keypad. Nobody is drowning, and no ship is sinking. What she has is an old man, a dying battery, and a goodbye that nobody is going to hear, and the recording has no button for that. It begins to repeat itself.

choices.label: Press one for the duty controller.
Leave a message after the tone.

nodes.body: She presses one, and the duty controller picks up sounding like a man hauled out of the bottom of a well, though he is wide awake by her third sentence. "Kell's KX is still up?" he says. "Stay on the line." She hears switches, a chair, and then his voice gone flat and official as he puts the call across the county net: all stations, a message for Marin Alder, repeat it on your own frequencies. Replies start coming in before he has finished, a dozen voices treading on one another, and most of them are only confirming. One is a woman two ridges west who will not give a call sign, and who keeps asking what the message says. "It could be nothing," the controller tells Wren, "and I can patch you through to her, but then I cannot log the others, and I have nineteen minutes of others."

choices.label: Ask him to patch her through to the woman.
Help him log every reply.

nodes.body: "Patch me through to her," Wren says, and there is a click, and then a silence with somebody breathing in it. "My name is Wren, and I'm nobody, I only heard him." She tells the rest as plainly as she can. On the other end a woman who has sat up beside a radio every winter for thirty years, without once touching the key, begins to laugh and cry at the same time. "I read those numbers for him when I was seventeen," Marin Alder says. "All this time I have been listening to myself asking me to come home." The controller is already calling KX by name, over and over, until a microphone on the headland is picked up at last. The county net falls as silent as a church, and across it an old man's voice says, live and astonished, "Marin?"

"Log them," Wren says, "all of them, because we can't afford to lose one." So she reads back call signs while the controller writes, twenty-three stations in nineteen minutes. Each one promises to repeat the message at the top of every hour. At twenty to midnight the loop on the headland stops, and the net does not. "Marin Alder, Marin Alder, your father is asking for you," says a fishing boat off the point, and a hospital porter on his break, and a boy of eleven with a kit radio who ought to be asleep. Wren will never know which of them reaches her, or when. But a message that belonged to one tired man for thirty years has a hundred pairs of hands on it tonight, and none of them shows any sign of letting go.

She leaves a message after the tone, because nobody is in danger and she was brought up not to cry wolf. It is a good message. She gives the frequency, the time, the name Marin Alder, and her own telephone number, twice, slowly, and then she goes up to the attic and listens to the loop run down by herself. At six the next morning the telephone rings, and a man with a clipped controller's voice asks whether she is the young lady who called about KX. "I wish to heaven you had pressed one," he says. "We have had a listener two ridges west asking after that station every winter for eleven years, and never would she leave her name. Property was in danger, miss, thirty years of it." Wren is still holding the receiver when her alarm goes off for school.

She picks up the telephone and then stands holding it, because waking someone means knowing whom to wake. The tide table has the coast guard auxiliary's number printed along its bottom edge, and those people own trucks and radios and the right to cut a chain. They will want an emergency, though, and what she has is a sad story with a deadline. Her grandfather's address book is another matter. Somewhere in it, among forty years of radio friends, there ought to be a man who worked that relay before the county closed it, and who would not need one word explained. From the landing window she can see a single light still burning down at the marina. She has fifty-six minutes, a dial tone, and a thumb that will not stop shaking.

choices.label: Call the coast guard auxiliary.
Search the address book for a relay man.
Ring Mrs. Okafor at the marina.

nodes.body: Mrs. Okafor answers the marina telephone on the second ring, as if she had been sitting beside it all evening. "It is stopping, then," she says, before Wren has finished her first sentence, "so be at the end of your road in six minutes, and bring a coat." She drives an old flatbed truck the way she mends nets, without one wasted movement, and the gale shoves at it all the way out along the cliff. At the station she does not go near the chained gate, but takes the service road round to the back, climbs down, and pulls a key on a loop of twine from inside her collar. "Thirty years of leaving soup on that step," she says, "and he gave me this so that the gulls would not get to it first."

choices.label: Follow her through the door.

nodes.body: The steel door opens on a small warm room, and the old man at the console turns round with his headset half off. "Kell Alder," Mrs. Okafor says, "this is the Callahan girl, and she has heard every word you have put out, so now you are going to stop talking to a tape recorder." She picks up the address book that lies open beside the telephone and holds it in front of his face, with her thumb under a number circled so many times that the paper shines. "You have had this for six years, and tonight you will dial it." His hand shakes so badly that Wren has to read him the digits one at a time. Two ridges west a telephone rings, and rings, and is answered. "Marin, it's your father," the old man says, "and no, don't hang up, because it really is me this time." The red numbers on the console go on counting down, and nobody in the room is looking at them.

She calls the coast guard auxiliary, and a duty officer answers before the first ring has finished, in the voice of a man with a form in front of him and a pen in his hand. "Auxiliary, go ahead, caller." Wren has rehearsed nothing. All she can see is an old man in a warm room beside a guttering cell, and all she can hear is that careful voice counting, and the whole story is crowding up behind her teeth at once. "Caller, are you still there?" the officer says. "I need a location from you, and then I need the nature of the emergency, in that order."

choices.label: Give him a location, a hazard, and a time.
Tell him the whole story from the beginning.

nodes.body: She gives him a location, a hazard, and a time, in that order: the old relay on the headland, an old man alone in it with a gale coming, and twenty to midnight. The officer's voice changes before she has finished, and she hears keys clattering. "Twenty to midnight is the top of a spring tide tonight, and with that gale behind it the sea will be in that yard," he says. "Occupied building, headland, spring tide plus gale, stand by." Eleven minutes later a crew chief is on the line from a truck, shouting over the engine, while Wren talks him round the chained gate and down the service road with a map spread under her elbows. "We're in," the chief says. "One male, elderly, uninjured, and not best pleased to see us. There's a console in here counting down, and he says it is none of our business. I've got sandbags and a generator, and I've got a records clerk on the radio who can find anybody in the county, but I have hands for one job before that tide tops out. So which is it to be, miss?"

choices.label: Tell him to find a number for Marin.
Tell him to sandbag the building and run the generator.

nodes.body: "Find a number for Marin Alder," Wren says, "two ridges west, and put her through to that room." The clerk has it in four minutes, which the chief says is a personal record. Wren hears all of it down the truck's open line: a telephone ringing far away, a woman's sleepy hello, and then the chief's big voice gone unexpectedly careful. "Ma'am, I am standing in a radio station with your father, and he has something he would like to say to you himself." There is a long pause with the gale in it. "Kell," the chief says, away from the phone, "she's on, and she says to tell you she can hear you fine." By then the sea is in the yard and the tapes are up on a high shelf, and nobody in the building cares about either.

"Sandbag the building," Wren says, "and save the tapes and the power, all of it, because if that station dies there is nothing left for her to find." The chief does not argue. For half an hour she listens to sandbags thumping down and a generator coughing into life. At twenty to midnight she hears the old man himself, close to the phone, say gruffly, "The HOLD switch, under the red guard, no, the other red guard." The count stops with four seconds showing. In the morning the auxiliary opens a missing-relative file for one Marin Alder, last known two ridges west. The officer who takes it on has thirty years of recordings to play her when he finds her. He rings the Callahan house first, to say thank you, and to ask how a schoolgirl knew to give him the place, the danger and the hour before anything else.

She tells him the whole story from the beginning, the attic and the numbers and the thirty years, and she can hear his pen stop moving somewhere around the Morse chart. He is kind about it. "So nobody is in the water," he says, "and nobody has called for help, and what we have is a radio program that finishes at midnight." He takes her name, and it goes in the log, under the heading the auxiliary keeps for whales, strange lights, and bottles with letters in them. At twenty to midnight the sea comes over the wall at the relay station, with one old man inside and no truck on the road. He is found in the morning, cold and furious and unhurt, sweeping the tide back out of his doorway with a broom, among thirty years of ruined tape. The officer rings Wren himself. "Next time," he says, "start with the tide."

She searches the address book for a relay man and finds a page of them, under K for KX, in her grandfather's cramped capitals. Eight names are bracketed together, with a note beside the bracket: TRANSFERRED INLAND. Their numbers are long, with distant codes. Below the bracket, a line by itself carries the name Ruiz and a local number across the bay, and next to that her grandfather has printed three words: STAYED, WON'T TALK. Her watch says fifty-one minutes. Somewhere outside a shutter has come loose and is banging against the house, slow and regular, like a count.

choices.label: Dial Ruiz across the bay.
Work down the eight inland numbers.

nodes.body: She dials Ruiz across the bay, and he answers with his mouth full, and stops chewing at the word schedule. "So Kell has finally set the last one," he says, "and I always knew he would, the stubborn old fool. Where do you live?" Twenty-five minutes later a pickup truck with one working headlight is idling at the end of her road, and twenty after that it is nosed up against the back wall of the relay station, rocking in the gale. Ruiz kills the engine and takes a ring of keys down off the mirror, a small, square man with a voice like gravel in a bucket. "This is thirty years of two old men not talking to each other," he says, "and it will not be pretty. You have done your part, kid, so you can stay in the truck, where it is dry."

choices.label: Get out and go in with Ruiz.
Stay in the truck, as he says.

nodes.body: She gets out and goes in with Ruiz, and he does not tell her twice to stay behind. The old man at the console turns round, sees who it is, and says a word that Wren pretends not to hear. "You owe me thirty years of conversation, Kell," Ruiz says, hanging up his coat as if he had left yesterday. "This is the Callahan girl, and she has been listening, which is more than I ever had the nerve to do." It takes all three of them. Ruiz strips a spare cell out of the mast heater and wires it across the dying one, the old man holds the count, and Wren, because hers are the steadiest hands in the room, dials the number circled in his address book. When a woman's voice answers, both men reach for the telephone at once, and it is Ruiz who lets go.

She stays in the truck, as he says, with the heater ticking and the rain coming sideways across the one good headlight. Ruiz lets himself in at the back door, and for a long time nothing happens that she can see. At twenty to midnight the mast lamp goes out, and comes on again, and goes out, and Wren presses her face to the cold window and cannot tell what any of it means. It is nearly one when Ruiz climbs back in, smelling of solder, and starts the engine without a word. "Tell me whether she answered," Wren says. He drives a full mile before he says, "He asked who was in the truck, and I am to tell you that the door is open in daylight, and that some things a person ought to hear from the man himself." She was thirty yards from the end of the story, with the heater on.

She works down the eight inland numbers, one after another, because eight chances must be better than one. Two are disconnected, one is a laundry, and one belongs to a widow who is very sorry, dear, and who would like to talk about her husband for as long as Wren will let her. The seventh is answered by an old man who listens to the whole story in silence. "You want Ruiz," he says, "because the rest of us took the money and went. Ruiz bought a house across the bay, where he could see that mast lamp from his kitchen, and he has watched it every night since, and he still has his keys." Wren looks at her watch. It is nine minutes to midnight, and the lamp he has been watching went out eleven minutes ago.
